sentences.text: Mimodactylus is a pterodactyloid pterosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Lebanon, representing the first complete pterosaur discovered from the Afro-Arabian continent.

The holotype specimen, which was far from fully developed, had a preserved skull measuring 99 mm in length and a preserved lower jaw measuring 105 mm, while the total wingspan reached 132 centimeters.

Its skull featured a wide snout that ended in a sharp point rather than a rounded front, and the animal possessed a very short tail evidenced by seven visible caudal vertebrae that quickly diminished in size towards the rear.
Unfused bones in the specimen indicate that the animal was likely a juvenile when it died.
This specimen holds the distinction of being the first complete pterosaur discovered from the Afro-Arabian continent.
Mimodactylus was the first istiodactyliform discovered in Gondwana, whereas other members of the group were previously known only from Early Cretaceous sites in Europe and Asia.
The specimen was collected from a private quarry near Hjoula, Lebanon, over fifteen years before it was scientifically described in 2019.

The only known specimen was found in a limestone quarry near Hjoula in the Sannine Formation, and the species Mimodactylus libanensis was named and described in 2019 by Alexander Wilhelm Armin Kellner, Michael Wayne Caldwell, Borja Holgado, Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia, Roy Nohra, Juliana Manso Sayão, and Philip John Currie.

In 2019, Dany Azar and colleagues reported fossil dragonflies and a beetle from Hjoula, showing the site has potential for preserving insects, though when Mimodactylus was described, insects had not been discovered at Hjoula and terrestrial plant fossils were very rare there.

Researchers suggested in 2019 that Mimodactylus likely had unique feeding habits distinct from other pterosaurs, possessing a broad rostrum and widely spaced, robust, pointed teeth adapted for seizing shrimp in the water.

Researchers noted that while insectivory could not be ruled out, Mimodactylus's broad rostrum was consistent with a primarily crustacean diet, similar to extant ducks, boat-billed herons, and shoebills, as the site is rich in crustacean fossils belonging to the order Decapoda that could have been scooped from the water surface by the wide beak.

Its short, straight, non-serrated conical teeth would have been useful for breaking the exoskeletons of arthropods, which could indicate it was an insectivore, but insects are absent from the Lagerstätte layers.

Mimodactylus likely had limited maneuverability during flight but was highly stable, similar to albatrosses and other open-sea fliers, suggesting that dynamic soaring, flying with little flapping, may have been the mode of flight for large pterosaurs including Mimodactylus.
Its elongated wings did not provide the maneuverability needed to catch fast-flying insects, but would allow stable flight during dynamic flight over the sea surface.
The genus Mimodactylus was established by Kellner et al. in 2019, and the parent group of Mimodactylus is the family Mimodactylidae.

Kellner and colleagues named the clade containing Mimodactylus and Haopterus Mimodactylidae within the group Lanceodontia, and in 2019, Mimodactylus was placed within the clade Lanceodontia and the Istiodactyliformes.
Mimodactylus lived in present-day Lebanon during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 95 million years ago, specifically during the late Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous.
Mimodactylus lived during the Cenomanian stage, between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.

A 2021 study by Jiang Shunxing and colleagues placed Mimodactylus in an unresolved polytomy with Haopterus, Yixianopterus, and Linlongopterus, whereas in 2022, Yizhi Xu and colleagues classified Mimodactylus as the sister taxon of Linlongopterus, with Haopterus at the base of their clade.
It is debated whether Mimodactylus was insectivorous, as insectivorous pterosaurs like anurognathids typically have slim, well-spaced, isodont teeth.
The pteroid bone points clearly towards the neck and articulates with the proximal syncarpus; this had been a point of discussion among researchers.
